content: Hereditary sensory neuropathy type II, also referred to as HSN2, is a protein encoded by the HSN2 gene in humans. This gene is a single-exon open reading frame (ORF) and represents a nervous system-specific exon of the WNK1 gene. HSN2 functions as an alternatively spliced exon of WNK1, and this splicing event occurs selectively in nervous tissues. As a result, it gives rise to WNK1/HSN2 isoforms that are specific to the nervous system. The WNK1/HSN2 isoforms are predominantly expressed in sensory regions of both the peripheral nervous system (PNS) and the central nervous system (CNS). These regions are involved in the transmission of sensory and nociceptive signals, which include the perception of pain. Specific cellular components where these isoforms are expressed include satellite cells, Schwann cells, and sensory neurons. The protein product of this isoform is found in higher concentrations in sensory neurons compared to motor neurons. It is hypothesized that this protein may play a critical role in the development and/or maintenance of peripheral sensory neurons or their supporting Schwann cells. Mutations in the HSN2 gene are linked to a condition known as congenital sensory neuropathy, specifically hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy type II (HSAN Type II). This is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by a significant reduction or complete absence of peripheral sensory neurons. Clinically, this results in impaired sensations of pain, temperature, and touch.
